quests.hint: Scope questions work best when you offer a specific either/or. Vague questions get vague answers.
quests.explanation: Naming the two possibilities ('mobile app or only the website') forces a clear decision at the start of a project. It prevents the costly situation where each person assumes a different scope.
quests.situationText: It's the kickoff meeting for a client project. Everyone is talking about deadlines, but nobody has said whether the mobile app is part of the first phase.
quests.sampleAnswer: Before we start, could we agree on what's in scope? Does the first phase include the mobile app, or just the website?
quests.correctAnswer: Before we begin, can we confirm the scope? Does the first phase include the mobile app, or only the website?
acceptedSynonyms: I'd like to check what's included in phase one. Are we building the app as well, or only the website?
Could we clarify the scope before we go further? Is the mobile app part of the first phase?
Before we begin, can we confirm the scope? Does the first phase include the mobile app, or only the website?
Just so we're all clear: does the first phase cover the mobile app, or just the website?

quests.hint: Ask for a definition of success in the client's terms. A number or date is more useful than a general aim.
quests.explanation: Asking what the client cares about most reveals priorities that shape every later decision. Offering examples ('a number or a date') helps them give a precise answer.
quests.situationText: Your team is starting a new project for a retail client. You've heard many goals, but you don't know which one will decide whether the client is happy.
quests.sampleAnswer: How will we know the project has been a success? Is there a number or a date the client cares about most?
quests.correctAnswer: How will we know the project has succeeded? Is there a specific number or date that matters most to the client?
acceptedSynonyms: How will we know the project has succeeded? Is there a specific number or date that matters most to the client?
What does success look like for the client? Is there a particular target or deadline they care about?
Which result matters most to them? Is it a sales figure, a launch date, or something else?
Could we agree on how success will be measured? Is there a key number or date for the client?

quests.hint: Money limits shape the whole plan. Ask whether the number is fixed, and mention what could change it.
quests.explanation: Asking 'is there flexibility if the scope grows?' raises the difficult topic early and calmly. It's easier to discuss at the start than after costs have increased.
quests.situationText: In a planning meeting for an office move, your manager mentions the budget once but doesn't say how strict it is. Extra requests from staff are already appearing.
quests.sampleAnswer: Is the budget fixed, or is there some flexibility if the scope grows?
quests.correctAnswer: Do we have a fixed budget, or is there some flexibility if the scope grows?
acceptedSynonyms: Is that budget a hard limit, or could it increase if more requirements come up?
Could you tell me how firm the budget is? What happens if the scope expands?
Do we have a fixed budget, or is there some flexibility if the scope grows?
Is there any room in the budget if people keep adding requests?

quests.hint: Present the conflict as a fact and ask the decision-maker to choose. Don't pick a side yourself.
quests.explanation: Telling your manager that two urgent tasks can't both be done by Friday puts the choice where it belongs. 'Which should I do first?' avoids blame and gets a clear priority.
quests.situationText: Two different managers have each sent you a task marked 'urgent' this morning. You calculate that you can only finish one by Friday.
quests.sampleAnswer: I've been given two urgent tasks, and there's only time for one before Friday. Which one has priority?
quests.correctAnswer: Both of these are marked urgent, but I can't finish both by Friday. Which should I do first?
acceptedSynonyms: Both of these are marked urgent, but I can't finish both by Friday. Which should I do first?
I've been given two urgent tasks, and there's only time for one before Friday. Which one has priority?
These two requests clash. Could you tell me which is more important so I can plan properly?
I can't complete both by Friday. Which one would you like me to focus on?

quests.hint: Say yes in principle, but explain the constraint with a time. Offer a specific moment when you'll be free.
quests.explanation: A time-limited offer ('after three') shows willingness while protecting your deadline. It's much better than a vague 'I'm busy'.
quests.situationText: A teammate asks if you can review her presentation right now. You're in the middle of finishing a report due at three.
quests.sampleAnswer: Happy to help once I've finished this report at three. Would that be okay?
quests.correctAnswer: I'd like to help, but I'm on a deadline until three. Could I have a look after that?
acceptedSynonyms: I want to give this proper attention, and I'm busy until three. Would after three suit you?
I can do it, but not right now. I have a report due at three. Could I read it afterwards?
I'd like to help, but I'm on a deadline until three. Could I have a look after that?
Happy to help once I've finished this report at three. Would that be okay?

quests.hint: Accept new work by naming the consequence for the old work. Ask whether it's acceptable.
quests.explanation: Showing the trade-off ('the report will slip to Thursday') lets your manager make an informed decision. Agreeing to help without mentioning the impact can create problems later.
quests.situationText: Your manager asks you to prepare a client presentation by Wednesday. You're already working on a report due the same day. The report would then be finished on Thursday.
quests.sampleAnswer: I can take that on, but it means the report will slip to Thursday. Are you comfortable with that?
quests.correctAnswer: I can take that on, but the report will slip to Thursday. Is that acceptable?
acceptedSynonyms: I can take that on, but the report will slip to Thursday. Is that acceptable?
Yes, I can do the presentation, though the report would then be a day late. Is that all right?
I'm able to do both, but not on the same day. The report would move to Thursday. Would that work?
I'm happy to help, but something has to give. The report would be finished on Thursday instead. Is that okay?

quests.hint: State the cause, the new date, and ask whether it works. The reason makes the request credible.
quests.explanation: Giving the cause ('a problem with the data') and a firm new date shows control of the situation. Asking 'Would that work?' invites cooperation rather than demanding forgiveness.
quests.situationText: Your team promised a client a report by the fifteenth. A problem with the data means you need five more days.
quests.sampleAnswer: We've hit a problem with the data, so we'd need until the twentieth instead of the fifteenth. Would that work for you?
quests.correctAnswer: We've run into a data problem, so we'd need until the twentieth rather than the fifteenth. Would that work for you?
acceptedSynonyms: Unfortunately, there's an issue with the data. Could we deliver on the twentieth instead of the fifteenth?
We've run into a data problem, so we'd need until the twentieth rather than the fifteenth. Would that work for you?
We need a little more time because of a problem with the data. Would the twentieth be acceptable?
The data problem has delayed us. Is it possible to move the deadline from the fifteenth to the twentieth?

quests.hint: Offer a partial delivery if the client can't move the date. A smaller version on time is often better than all of it late.
quests.explanation: Splitting the delivery gives the client something on the original date and protects the relationship. Asking 'Would that be acceptable?' checks that the compromise meets their needs.
quests.situationText: The client says the fifteenth cannot change. You can't complete everything by then, but the main features could be ready.
quests.sampleAnswer: If we need to keep the fifteenth, we could deliver the main features first and add the rest afterwards. Would that be acceptable?
quests.correctAnswer: If the fifteenth can't change, we could deliver the main features first and add the rest later. Would that be acceptable?
acceptedSynonyms: We could meet the fifteenth with the essential features and complete the remainder afterwards. Does that suit you?
Would you accept the core functions on the fifteenth and the rest a week later?
Keeping the date is possible if we release the key features first. Would that be all right?
If the fifteenth can't change, we could deliver the main features first and add the rest later. Would that be acceptable?

quests.hint: State the gap ('two weeks later') as a fact, then ask for a partial delivery. Solutions matter more than blame.
quests.explanation: Stating the exact difference ('two weeks later') is factual, not emotional. Asking for a partial delivery is a practical way to reduce the harm without starting an argument.
quests.situationText: A supplier emails to say your order will arrive two weeks after the agreed date. You need at least some of the goods for a launch event.
quests.sampleAnswer: That's two weeks later than we agreed. Is it possible to deliver part of the order by the original date?
quests.correctAnswer: That's two weeks later than agreed. Can you deliver part of the order by the original date?
acceptedSynonyms: Two weeks is a serious delay for us. Could you send at least part of the order on time?
That's two weeks later than agreed. Can you deliver part of the order by the original date?
We were counting on the original date. Can you split the delivery so some of it arrives on time?
This delay is a problem for our event. Is a partial shipment by the original date possible?

quests.hint: Praise before requesting. A small addition, stated with a benefit, is easier to accept than a large change.
quests.explanation: Presenting the addition as a benefit for a specific reader ('the executives') makes it a shared goal. Saying 'nearly there' encourages, rather than criticizes.
quests.situationText: A colleague has sent you a report that's almost ready, but it starts directly with details. You know the executives who'll read it want a quick overview.
quests.sampleAnswer: The report is nearly there. Could you add a summary at the top? I think it would help the executives.
quests.correctAnswer: The report is nearly there. Could you add a short summary at the top? It'll help the executives.
acceptedSynonyms: The report is nearly there. Could you add a short summary at the top? It'll help the executives.
This looks good. Would you mind adding a summary at the beginning? The executives will appreciate it.
Great work so far. Could we put a brief summary up front for the executives?
It's almost finished. One suggestion: a summary at the top would help the senior readers.

quests.hint: Give a reason grounded in users, not taste. 'Some people may struggle' turns opinion into a fact worth checking.
quests.explanation: Framing the request in terms of user needs makes it less personal. 'Could we try…?' invites experimentation, which designers find less threatening than an order.
quests.situationText: A designer shows you a mock-up of a new app. You like it, but the button text is small, and many of your customers are older.
quests.sampleAnswer: I like the layout. Could we try a bigger font on the buttons? Some older users may struggle to read them.
quests.correctAnswer: I like the layout. Could we try larger text on the buttons? Some older users might find it hard to read.
acceptedSynonyms: The design is good. Would it be possible to increase the button font size? Older customers may have trouble with it.
Nice layout. Could we test bigger buttons? A lot of our users are older.
I like the layout. Could we try larger text on the buttons? Some older users might find it hard to read.
I'm happy with most of it. Can we make the button text larger for older users?

quests.hint: Report the behavior you observed and suggest a specific change. Avoid words that imply blame.
quests.explanation: Saying 'I noticed the form accepts…' describes the system, not the developer's mistake. Proposing a specific change gives the developer a clear task.
quests.situationText: While testing a website, you see that customers can submit the form with no name. You message the developer.
quests.sampleAnswer: I noticed the form accepts empty names. Would it be possible to require a name before it submits?
quests.correctAnswer: I noticed that the form accepts empty names. Could we make a name required before it submits?
acceptedSynonyms: I noticed that the form accepts empty names. Could we make a name required before it submits?
While testing, I found that the form goes through without a name. Could it require one?
The form lets people submit without a name. Would you mind adding a check for that?
I spotted that empty names are accepted. Is it possible to make the field mandatory?

quests.hint: Propose a pattern and show it won't harm team needs. A schedule that protects meetings is easier to approve.
quests.explanation: Suggesting which days you'd be in the office, and connecting them to team meetings, shows that you have thought about the team, not only yourself.
quests.situationText: You'd like to work from home two days a week. Your team has important meetings on Monday and Tuesday. You'd like Wednesdays and Fridays.
quests.sampleAnswer: Would it be possible to work from home on Wednesdays and Fridays? I'd be in the office for team meetings on Monday and Tuesday.
quests.correctAnswer: Would it be possible for me to work from home on Wednesdays and Fridays? I'd be in the office on Mondays and Tuesdays for the team meetings.
acceptedSynonyms: I'd like to ask about remote work on Wednesdays and Fridays. I'd come in for our Monday and Tuesday meetings.
Would it be possible for me to work from home on Wednesdays and Fridays? I'd be in the office on Mondays and Tuesdays for the team meetings.
Could I work from home two days a week, Wednesday and Friday? I'd make sure to attend all team meetings in the office.
Is there any chance of working remotely on Wednesdays and Fridays? I'd be here Monday and Tuesday for meetings.

quests.hint: A personal reason can support a schedule request when it's brief and the change is small. Specify the exact hours.
quests.explanation: Precise hours ('eight to four') let your manager see the exact effect. A brief family reason is enough and doesn't require details.
quests.situationText: You'd like to move your hours to eight-to-four so that you can pick up your daughter from school. You speak to your manager.
quests.sampleAnswer: Could I shift my hours to eight-to-four? It would let me pick up my daughter from school.
quests.correctAnswer: Could I change my hours to eight until four? It would let me collect my daughter from school.
acceptedSynonyms: Would it be possible to start at eight and finish at four? I need to pick up my daughter.
I'd like to ask about working eight to four. School pick-up is the reason.
Is it all right if I start earlier and leave at four? It'd help with my daughter's school hours.
Could I change my hours to eight until four? It would let me collect my daughter from school.

quests.hint: Trade holidays or time with a colleague by offering the return favor up front.
quests.explanation: 'If I take…, I can cover…' presents a fair exchange so the colleague doesn't feel they lose out. It turns a competition for popular dates into cooperation.
quests.situationText: You and a colleague both want the first week of July as holiday, but the office can't be empty. You'd be happy to work the following week instead.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'd love the first week of July, and I'd happily cover you the week after. Would you be okay with that?
quests.correctAnswer: If I take the first week of July, I can cover the second week for you. Would that work?
acceptedSynonyms: I'd love the first week of July, and I'd happily cover you the week after. Would you be okay with that?
If I take the first week of July, I can cover the second week for you. Would that work?
How about I take the first week and cover your desk in the second? Does that suit you?
Could we split it? I'll take the first week of July and cover for you the second.

quests.hint: Use an everyday comparison to explain a technical problem. The picture matters more than the exact vocabulary.
quests.explanation: Analogies replace jargon with something the listener already understands. A 'shop with one cashier' immediately shows why more capacity is needed.
quests.situationText: You must explain to a non-technical director why the website crashes during sales. The problem is that too many users arrive at once.
quests.sampleAnswer: Imagine one cashier serving a huge queue. That's our website when there are too many visitors, which is why we need more capacity.
quests.correctAnswer: The system can't handle so many users at once, like a shop with one cashier and a long queue. We need more capacity.
acceptedSynonyms: It's a bit like a busy shop with one till. When too many customers arrive at the same time, everything slows down, so we need to add capacity.
Imagine one cashier serving a huge queue. That's our website when there are too many visitors, which is why we need more capacity.
Our system is like a shop with a single cashier. During a sale, the queue gets too long, so we need to increase the capacity.
The system can't handle so many users at once, like a shop with one cashier and a long queue. We need more capacity.

quests.hint: Give the customer the cause in plain words, then the practical consequence. Don't hide it behind technical terms.
quests.explanation: Customers want to know why and how long. 'Backorder' is explained by 'the part isn't available yet', and the extra week gives them a concrete expectation.
quests.situationText: You work at a repair shop. A customer's appliance can't be fixed because a needed part is out of stock at the supplier.
quests.sampleAnswer: We're waiting for a part that isn't in stock yet, so it will take roughly a week more than planned.
quests.correctAnswer: The part we need is on backorder, so the repair will take about a week longer than we told you.
acceptedSynonyms: We're waiting for a part that isn't in stock yet, so it will take roughly a week more than planned.
The part we need is on backorder, so the repair will take about a week longer than we told you.
I'm sorry, the supplier is out of the part we need. That will add about a week to the repair.
The part has been delayed by the supplier. Realistically, the repair will take around a week longer.

quests.hint: Explain a numbers discrepancy by identifying the difference in process, not a mistake. Keep the sentence simple.
quests.explanation: Saying 'count the same sale on different days' explains why the figures differ without suggesting someone made an error. Non-financial listeners can follow a simple cause.
quests.situationText: Two departments report different totals for last month's sales. You have found that they record the same sale on different days. You explain it to the director.
quests.sampleAnswer: The numbers don't match because two departments count the same sale on different days.
quests.correctAnswer: The figures differ because the two departments record the same sale on different days.
acceptedSynonyms: It's not an error. Sales and finance simply record a sale on different dates, which changes the monthly total.
The totals are different because each department has its own way of dating a sale.
The gap comes from timing. One team counts a sale when it's made, and the other when it's paid.
The figures differ because the two departments record the same sale on different days.

quests.hint: Present two options by naming the cost and the benefit of each. Then invite a decision.
quests.explanation: 'Faster but costs more' versus 'cheaper but takes longer' shows a real trade-off in one sentence each. It prepares the manager to decide without further discussion.
quests.situationText: Your team is behind on a design task. You can either hire a freelancer or do the work yourselves, and you must explain both to your manager.
quests.sampleAnswer: We could hire a freelancer, which is faster but costs more, or do it ourselves, which is cheaper but takes longer.
quests.correctAnswer: We could hire a freelancer, which would be faster but more expensive, or do it ourselves, which is cheaper but slower.
acceptedSynonyms: There are two options. A freelancer would speed things up but cost more, while doing it ourselves saves money but takes longer.
We can pay for a freelancer and finish sooner, or handle it in-house and save money at the cost of time.
We could hire a freelancer, which would be faster but more expensive, or do it ourselves, which is cheaper but slower.
One choice is quicker and pricier, with a freelancer. The other is cheaper and slower, if we do it ourselves.

quests.hint: Give a recommendation after describing the options. Say why it fits this particular situation.
quests.explanation: Ending with your own suggestion and a reason ('given the client') shows judgment. Managers value people who not only list options but also choose between them.
quests.situationText: You've compared two ways to migrate a client's data. One is slower but safer, and the other is faster but has a small risk of errors. The client is very sensitive about accuracy.
quests.sampleAnswer: Option A is safer but slower. Option B is faster, but there's a small risk of errors. Given the client, I'd suggest A.
quests.correctAnswer: Option A is safer but slower, and option B is faster with a small risk of errors. I'd suggest A, given this client.
acceptedSynonyms: Option A is safer but slower, and option B is faster with a small risk of errors. I'd suggest A, given this client.
I see two options. A is slower but safer, and B is quicker but might contain errors. For this client, I'd recommend A.
A is safer, though it takes longer. B saves time, but errors are possible. Considering the client, A seems better.
We can choose between a slower, safer method and a faster, riskier one. Because of who the client is, I'd go with the safer one.

quests.hint: Describe the compromise and its cost honestly. A recommendation that hides its downside isn't trusted.
quests.explanation: Being open about the downside ('less useful') builds credibility. It also lets the decision-maker weigh the price reduction against the effect on customers.
quests.situationText: Your company wants to reduce the price of a product. The only way is to remove some extra features, which some customers like.
quests.sampleAnswer: We could lower the price by dropping the extra features. The trade-off is that customers may find it less useful.
quests.correctAnswer: We could reduce the price by dropping the extra features. The downside is that customers might find the product less useful.
acceptedSynonyms: Removing the extras would let us cut the price, but some customers may see less value in it.
One way to lower the price is to take out the additional features, though it could make the product less attractive.
We could reduce the price by dropping the extra features. The downside is that customers might find the product less useful.
We can cut the cost by removing the extra features. The price we pay is that some people may find it less useful.

quests.hint: Ask directly who owns a task, and give a reason for asking. It sounds neutral when you name the risk.
quests.explanation: Naming the risk ('fall through the cracks') shows that you're asking to protect the project, not to shift work. Directly stating both names avoids assumptions.
quests.situationText: You and a colleague finished a document together, but neither of you has mentioned who will send it to the client on Friday.
quests.sampleAnswer: Who's responsible for sending the final version to the client, you or me? I want to make sure it doesn't fall through the cracks.
quests.correctAnswer: Who's going to send the final version to the client, you or me? I don't want it to fall through the cracks.
acceptedSynonyms: Who's going to send the final version to the client, you or me? I don't want it to fall through the cracks.
Just to be clear, who's sending the final version to the client? I'd hate for it to get forgotten.
Can we decide who will send the final document to the client? I want to be sure it goes out.
Whose job is it to send the client the final version? I'd like us to be clear so nothing is missed.

quests.hint: Divide the work aloud and check that you both agree. Restating shared responsibilities prevents later conflict.
quests.explanation: Saying who does what, and asking 'Is that how you see it?', turns an assumption into an agreement. It's a quick habit that avoids the frustrations of duplicated or forgotten work.
quests.situationText: Your colleague and you are preparing a joint presentation. You assume you'll do the slides and she'll prepare the figures, but you haven't said so.
quests.sampleAnswer: Shall we make sure we agree? I'll build the slides, and you'll do the numbers.
quests.correctAnswer: Just so we're clear, I'll handle the slides, and you'll prepare the figures. Is that how you see it?
acceptedSynonyms: Let me confirm who's doing what. I'll take the slides and you take the figures. Does that match your understanding?
So I'm on the slides, and you're on the figures? Have I got that right?
Just so we're clear, I'll handle the slides, and you'll prepare the figures. Is that how you see it?
Shall we make sure we agree? I'll build the slides, and you'll do the numbers.

quests.hint: If you're blamed for something outside your role, say so factually and move to a solution.
quests.explanation: Stating that you weren't involved without becoming defensive keeps the discussion calm. Offering help and asking who to involve turns the problem into something to solve together.
quests.situationText: In a meeting, a manager says that a mistake in a customer contract was your fault, but the decision was made by another team.
quests.sampleAnswer: I wasn't involved in that decision, but I'm happy to help fix it. Who should we talk to?
quests.correctAnswer: I wasn't part of that decision, but I'm happy to help put it right. Who should we speak to?
acceptedSynonyms: I wasn't part of that decision, but I'm happy to help put it right. Who should we speak to?
That decision was made by another team, though I'd like to help resolve it. Who's the right person to talk to?
I wasn't involved in the contract, but I'll help fix the problem. Who should we contact?
I don't think that was my decision, but let's find a solution. Who handled it?

quests.hint: Summarize both understandings neutrally, then invite correction. It defuses the situation.
quests.explanation: Saying 'each understood differently' shares the responsibility for the confusion. Offering to summarize and asking to be corrected creates a way to reach a shared understanding.
quests.situationText: Two team members are arguing over a decision made last week. It's clear that each remembers it differently, and you're the one who wrote the notes.
quests.sampleAnswer: It looks as if there's been a misunderstanding. Let me go through what I noted, and you can correct me.
quests.correctAnswer: It sounds like we understood the decision differently. Let me summarize what I heard, and you tell me if I've got it wrong.
acceptedSynonyms: I think we remember the decision in different ways. Let me say what I understood, and please correct me.
It sounds like we understood the decision differently. Let me summarize what I heard, and you tell me if I've got it wrong.
We seem to have different versions of what was decided. Could I summarize mine, and you tell me where it differs?
It looks as if there's been a misunderstanding. Let me go through what I noted, and you can correct me.

quests.hint: Suggest a call when an email discussion goes in circles. Show that you agree more than it seems.
quests.explanation: Saying 'we're saying the same thing in different words' lowers the temperature. Proposing a call is a practical answer to written misunderstandings.
quests.situationText: You and a colleague have exchanged six emails about a deadline, and the tone is becoming sharper. You believe you both want the same result.
quests.sampleAnswer: We may agree more than these emails suggest. Would you be free for a short phone call?
quests.correctAnswer: I think we're actually saying the same thing in different words. Could we have a quick call to sort it out?
acceptedSynonyms: We may agree more than these emails suggest. Would you be free for a short phone call?
I feel we're on the same page but writing past each other. Can we talk it through by phone?
This is getting complicated by email. Could we have a five-minute call to clear it up?
I think we're actually saying the same thing in different words. Could we have a quick call to sort it out?

quests.hint: Close a confusing meeting by confirming action items. Ask for names and dates.
quests.explanation: Ending a meeting with 'who is doing what by when' is the most effective way to prevent later confusion. 'On the same page' is a common phrase for shared understanding.
quests.situationText: A long meeting is ending, and several tasks were discussed, but no one said who'd do them. People are packing up.
quests.sampleAnswer: Before we leave, can we confirm who's doing what by when? I'd like to be sure we're all on the same page.
quests.correctAnswer: Before we finish, could we confirm who's doing what and by when? I want to be sure we're all on the same page.
acceptedSynonyms: Sorry, before everyone goes, could we go through the actions and who owns them?
Before we finish, could we confirm who's doing what and by when? I want to be sure we're all on the same page.
Let's quickly recap the next steps, with names and dates, so nobody leaves unsure.
Could we take a minute to agree on who does what and by when before we close?

quests.hint: Acknowledge the emotion first, apologize for the effect, and then promise action. This order calms people down.
quests.explanation: Customers often need to hear that you understand before they listen to a solution. Promising to act 'today' shows you take responsibility, which builds trust.
quests.situationText: A customer phones, angry because her order arrived damaged and the first replacement was late as well. You're the customer service agent.
quests.sampleAnswer: I completely understand your frustration, and I'm sorry for the inconvenience. Let me see what I can do to fix this today.
quests.correctAnswer: I understand how frustrating this is, and I'm sorry for the inconvenience. Let me see what I can do to sort it out today.
acceptedSynonyms: I'm sorry you've had this experience. It must be very annoying. I'll do my best to resolve it today.
That sounds really frustrating, and I apologize. Let me look into it and find a solution today.
I can see why you're upset, and I'm sorry. Let me see how we can put this right straight away.
I understand how frustrating this is, and I'm sorry for the inconvenience. Let me see what I can do to sort it out today.

quests.hint: Start with the limit, then move quickly to what you can do. Two options give the customer some control.
quests.explanation: Starting with the limit, 'I'm afraid', is honest, and moving quickly to options prevents the customer from feeling stuck. Two alternatives give the customer some control.
quests.situationText: A customer wants a full refund for a sofa that he used for two months, which is outside your store's policy.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm afraid I can't offer a full refund, but I can offer a replacement or store credit. Would either of those help?
quests.correctAnswer: I'm afraid I can't give a full refund, but I can offer a replacement or a credit. Would either of those work for you?
acceptedSynonyms: Unfortunately a full refund isn't possible, but I could arrange an exchange or credit. Would that be suitable?
I'm afraid I can't give a full refund, but I can offer a replacement or a credit. Would either of those work for you?
I'm sorry, refunds aren't available at this stage. Could I offer you a replacement or store credit instead?
A full refund is outside our policy, but we can offer either a replacement or a credit. Which would you prefer?

quests.hint: With a customer who is shouting, stay calm, state your aim, and ask for the story in order.
quests.explanation: Saying that you want to help and how you can do it best sets a cooperative tone. Asking for the story from the beginning gives the customer a chance to vent while you gather facts.
quests.situationText: A customer in your shop starts shouting about a wrong bill. Other customers are looking.
